name: Two Pointers
description: Use two indices moving toward each other (or in the same direction) to solve problems in-place or find pairs.
whenToUse: Sorted array, find pair with target sum, remove duplicates, palindrome check, container with most water.
intuition: Two fingers on the array. If it's sorted and you want a pair summing to target, a left and right finger squeeze inward: sum too big, move right inward; too small, move left inward. You never revisit pairs you've ruled out, so it's O(n) instead of O(n^2).

name: Sliding Window
description: Maintain a window (subarray/substring) and expand/shrink it to find an optimal subarray satisfying a constraint.
spaceComplexity: O(k) where k = window size or charset
template:
from collections import defaultdict

def sliding_window(s, k):
    left = 0
    window = defaultdict(int)  # or use a sum variable
    result = 0

    for right in range(len(s)):
        # 1. Expand: add s[right] to window
        window[s[right]] += 1

        # 2. Shrink: while window is invalid
        while len(window) > k:          # condition depends on problem
            window[s[left]] -= 1
            if window[s[left]] == 0:
                del window[s[left]]
            left += 1

        # 3. Update result
        result = max(result, right - left + 1)

    return result

# Fixed-size window (max sum of k elements):
def max_sum_k(arr, k):
    window_sum = sum(arr[:k])
    best = window_sum
    for i in range(k, len(arr)):
        window_sum += arr[i] - arr[i - k]
        best = max(best, window_sum)
    return best
whenToUse: Longest/shortest subarray or substring with a condition, max sum of k elements, minimum window substring.
intuition: A stretchy window over the array. Expand the right edge to include more; the moment the window breaks its constraint (too many distinct chars, sum too big), shrink from the left until it's valid again. Each element enters and leaves once, so O(n). The go-to for 'longest/shortest subarray or substring with property X'.

name: Binary Search
description: Eliminate half the search space each iteration. Works on sorted inputs or when there is a monotonic predicate.
whenToUse: Sorted array target search, search in rotated array, find first/last occurrence, binary search on answer.
intuition: Picture a monotonic condition over the search space: false false false | true true true, and you're hunting the boundary, the first true. Write a predicate check(mid) and binary-search it: if check(mid) keep left (hi = mid), else go right (lo = mid + 1). This 'binary search on the answer' cracks 'smallest X that works' problems (Koko eats bananas, minimum capacity), not just sorted lookups. Plain sorted-array search is the simplest case; searching a rotated sorted array is a cousin variant where at each step you detect which half is currently sorted and recurse into the right one.

name: Fast & Slow Pointers
description: Floyd's cycle detection. Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. They meet iff there is a cycle.
whenToUse: Detect cycle in linked list, find cycle start, find middle of list, find k-th element from end.
intuition: Two runners on a track at different speeds. On a linked list, a 2x runner laps a 1x runner if and only if there's a cycle (they collide). The same gap finds the middle: when fast reaches the end, slow sits at the midpoint. Turns cycle and middle questions into O(1) space.

name: BFS
description: Breadth-first search explores level by level. Use a queue. Optimal for shortest path in unweighted graphs.
whenToUse: Shortest path, level-order traversal, minimum steps to reach target, word ladder, 0-1 BFS.
intuition: Ripples from a stone dropped in a pond, spreading out level by level. A queue holds the current frontier; you pop a node and enqueue its neighbors. Because you reach nodes in order of distance, the FIRST time you touch the target is the shortest path (unweighted).

name: DFS
description: Depth-first search goes as deep as possible before backtracking. Use recursion or an explicit stack.
whenToUse: Connected components, path existence, cycles (directed/undirected), topological sort, tree problems.
intuition: Plunge as deep as possible down one path, then backtrack. A stack (or the call stack via recursion) remembers where to return. Ideal for exploring every path, connectivity, and tree traversals where you finish a whole branch before starting the next.

name: Backtracking
description: Explore all possibilities by building a candidate solution and abandoning it ("backtrack") as soon as it is determined it cannot lead to a valid solution.
whenToUse: Permutations, combinations, subsets, N-queens, Sudoku, word search.
intuition: DFS that builds a candidate one choice at a time and undoes the last choice at a dead end: choose, explore, un-choose. Picture a decision tree, at each node try every option, recurse, then remove it. Prune branches that can't possibly work to stay fast (permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku).

name: Dynamic Programming (Memoization)
description: Top-down DP: recursively solve subproblems and cache results to avoid recomputation.
whenToUse: Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure: Fibonacci, coin change, knapsack, LCS, edit distance.
intuition: Recursion plus a cache. Express the answer in terms of smaller subproblems; if you'd recompute the same subproblem, store its result the first time and look it up afterward. Top-down recipe: write the naive recursion, then add a memo keyed by the exact state.

name: Dynamic Programming (Tabulation)
description: Bottom-up DP: fill a table iteratively from base cases up to the answer.
spaceComplexity: O(n) or O(1) with rolling array
timeComplexity: O(n) or O(n²) depending on dimensions
whenToUse: Same as memoization but avoids recursion stack overflow and is often faster in practice.
intuition: Fill a table from the base cases upward. Nail down the state and the transition (how a cell depends on earlier cells), then iterate so every dependency is ready before you need it. Bottom-up, and often O(1) space when a cell only needs the previous row or last few cells.

name: Monotonic Stack
description: A stack that is always sorted (increasing or decreasing). Pop when invariant is broken, capturing next greater/smaller element.
template:
# Next Greater Element (monotonic decreasing stack)
def next_greater(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []  # stores indices
    for i, val in enumerate(arr):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] < val:
            idx = stack.pop()
            result[idx] = val
        stack.append(i)
    return result

# Next Smaller Element (monotonic increasing stack)
def next_smaller(arr):
    result = [-1] * len(arr)
    stack = []
    for i, val in enumerate(arr):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] > val:
            idx = stack.pop()
            result[idx] = val
        stack.append(i)
    return result

# Largest Rectangle in Histogram
def largest_rect(heights):
    stack, max_area = [], 0
    heights.append(0)  # sentinel
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1
            max_area = max(max_area, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return max_area
whenToUse: Next greater element, next smaller element, largest rectangle in histogram, trapping rain water, daily temperatures.
intuition: A stack you keep sorted (increasing or decreasing). When a new element breaks the order, pop until it fits, and each pop is exactly the moment you've found that popped element's 'next greater/smaller'. Turns next-greater-element and largest-rectangle into O(n).

name: Heap / Priority Queue
description: Python's heapq is a min-heap. Negate values for max-heap. Use for top-K, schedule by priority, merge K sorted lists.
template:
import heapq

# Min-heap basics
heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, 3)
heapq.heappush(heap, 1)
top = heapq.heappop(heap)   # returns 1
peek = heap[0]              # peek min

# Max-heap: negate values
heapq.heappush(heap, -val)
max_val = -heapq.heappop(heap)

# Top-K largest (min-heap of size k)
def top_k_largest(nums, k):
    heap = []
    for num in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, num)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return list(heap)

# K-th largest
import heapq
def kth_largest(nums, k):
    return heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1]

# Merge K sorted lists
def merge_k_sorted(lists):
    heap, result = [], []
    for i, lst in enumerate(lists):
        if lst:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lst[0], i, 0))
    while heap:
        val, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        result.append(val)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j+1], i, j+1))
    return result
whenToUse: Top-K elements, K-th largest, merge K sorted lists, Dijkstra, task scheduling, median of stream.
intuition: A magic bag that always hands you the current smallest (or largest) item next, in O(log n). Reach for it on 'top-K', 'kth largest', merging k sorted lists, or anything scheduled by priority, whenever you repeatedly need the extreme without fully sorting.

name: Union Find (DSU)
description: Disjoint Set Union supports near-O(1) find and union with path compression + union by rank.
whenToUse: Connected components, detect cycle in undirected graph, number of islands (dynamic), minimum spanning tree (Kruskal).
intuition: Items grouped into sets: find(x) returns the set's representative, union(a,b) merges two sets. With path compression and union by rank it's effectively O(1). The mental model is connected components, 'are these two in the same group?' and merging groups (islands, Kruskal's MST, cycle detection).

name: Trie
description: A prefix tree for efficient string insert, search, and prefix queries.
timeComplexity: O(m) per operation where m = word length
whenToUse: Word search, autocomplete, prefix matching, word dictionary, boggle, longest common prefix.
intuition: A tree where each edge is a letter, so words sharing a prefix share a path. Walking down from the root spells a word; a flag on a node marks a complete word. Prefix queries and autocomplete become O(word length) instead of scanning every word.

name: Topological Sort
description: Linear ordering of vertices in a DAG such that for every edge (u→v), u comes before v. Kahn's algorithm uses BFS with in-degree counts.
template:
from collections import deque

# Kahn's Algorithm (BFS-based)
def topo_sort_kahn(n, edges):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    in_degree = [0] * n
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
        in_degree[v] += 1

    queue = deque(i for i in range(n) if in_degree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            in_degree[neighbor] -= 1
            if in_degree[neighbor] == 0:
                queue.append(neighbor)

    return order if len(order) == n else []  # empty → cycle exists

# DFS-based (postorder)
def topo_sort_dfs(n, edges):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)

    visited, result = [0] * n, []  # 0=unvisited, 1=visiting, 2=done
    def dfs(node):
        if visited[node] == 1: return False  # cycle
        if visited[node] == 2: return True
        visited[node] = 1
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if not dfs(nb): return False
        visited[node] = 2
        result.append(node)
        return True

    for i in range(n):
        if visited[i] == 0 and not dfs(i):
            return []  # cycle
    return result[::-1]
whenToUse: Course schedule, build order, dependency resolution, detect cycle in directed graph.
intuition: Order tasks so every prerequisite comes before it (course schedule). Repeatedly grab a node with nothing left blocking it (in-degree 0), remove it, and decrement its neighbors. If you ever get stuck with nodes remaining, there's a cycle. It's just BFS/DFS on a DAG.

name: Dijkstra
description: Greedy shortest path algorithm for weighted graphs with non-negative edges. Uses a min-heap.
whenToUse: Shortest path in weighted graph, network delay time, cheapest flights within K stops (modified).
intuition: BFS where the frontier is a min-heap ordered by distance, so you always expand the closest unfinished node. Because nodes are finalized in increasing distance, the first time you pop the target you already have its shortest path (non-negative weights only).

name: Prefix Sum
description: Precompute cumulative sums for O(1) range sum queries.
template:
# 1D Prefix Sum
def build_prefix(arr):
    prefix = [0] * (len(arr) + 1)
    for i, val in enumerate(arr):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + val
    return prefix

def range_sum(prefix, l, r):  # inclusive [l, r], 0-indexed
    return prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]

# Subarray sum equals k (HashMap approach)
from collections import defaultdict
def subarray_sum_k(nums, k):
    count, curr, freq = 0, 0, defaultdict(int)
    freq[0] = 1
    for num in nums:
        curr += num
        count += freq[curr - k]
        freq[curr] += 1
    return count

# 2D Prefix Sum
def build_2d_prefix(mat):
    m, n = len(mat), len(mat[0])
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    for r in range(1, m + 1):
        for c in range(1, n + 1):
            dp[r][c] = mat[r-1][c-1] + dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] - dp[r-1][c-1]
    return dp

def query_2d(dp, r1, c1, r2, c2):  # inclusive, 0-indexed
    return dp[r2+1][c2+1] - dp[r1][c2+1] - dp[r2+1][c1] + dp[r1][c1]
whenToUse: Subarray sum equals k, range sum queries, 2D range sums, product except self.
intuition: Precompute running totals so any range sum is a single subtraction: sum(i..j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]. Repeated range queries drop from O(n) each to O(1). 'Subarray sum equals k' is the same idea with a hashmap of prefix sums you've already seen.

name: Merge Intervals
description: Sort by start time, then merge overlapping intervals by comparing current end with next start.
whenToUse: Merge intervals, insert interval, meeting rooms, minimum meeting rooms (sweep line).
intuition: Sort by start, then sweep left to right: if the next interval overlaps the current one (next.start <= current.end), merge by stretching the end; otherwise close the current and open a new one. Nearly every interval problem begins with 'sort, then sweep'.

name: Matrix DFS/BFS (Islands)
description: Treat a 2D grid as a graph. DFS or BFS from each unvisited cell, marking visited to avoid cycles.
whenToUse: Number of islands, flood fill, max area of island, surrounded regions, shortest path in grid.
intuition: Treat the grid as a graph where each cell links to its 4 neighbors. Flood-fill from an unvisited land cell to sink the whole island (mark it visited), counting one island per flood. DFS or BFS both work.

name: HashMap / Frequency Counter
description: Use a hash map to count frequencies or store last seen indices. Eliminates the need for nested loops.
whenToUse: Two sum, group anagrams, first unique character, longest substring without repeat, valid anagram.
intuition: Trade space for time: a dictionary of counts or positions turns 'have I seen this, and how often' into O(1) lookups. Two-sum, anagram grouping, and dedup all collapse into 'just remember what you've seen'.

name: LRU Cache
description: Least Recently Used cache evicts the least recently accessed item. Implemented with a doubly linked list + hashmap for O(1) get & put.
whenToUse: System design (caching), interview implementation question.

name: Cyclic Sort
description: Place each number at its correct index by swapping. Works on arrays with values in range [1..n] or [0..n-1].
whenToUse: Find missing number, find duplicate, find all duplicates, smallest missing positive.
intuition: When values are a known range like 1..n, each value has a 'home' index (value v belongs at index v-1). Walk the array swapping each element to its home until everything sits in place. Now any index whose value is wrong reveals the missing/duplicate number, O(n) with no extra space.

name: Bit Manipulation
description: Operate directly on binary representations. XOR, AND, OR, shifts. Many tricks arise from bit-level properties.
timeComplexity: O(1) for most tricks, O(n) for array scans
whenToUse: Single number, missing number, subsets (bitmask DP), count bits, power of 2, swap without temp, gray code.

name: GCD, LCM & Euclidean Algorithm
description: Euclid's algorithm computes GCD in O(log min(a,b)). Key insight: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b).
whenToUse: Simplify fractions, find LCM, solve Diophantine equations, check if two numbers are coprime.

name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
description: Find all primes up to N in O(N log log N). Classic preprocessing for problems involving primes.
whenToUse: Count primes, prime factorisation, check primality for many numbers, Goldbach, twin primes.

name: Modular Arithmetic & Fast Exponentiation
description: Compute a^b mod m in O(log b) using repeated squaring. Essential for combinatorics, hashing, and cryptography problems.
template:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

# Fast power (built-in in Python: pow(a, b, mod))
def fast_pow(base, exp, mod):
    result = 1
    base %= mod
    while exp > 0:
        if exp & 1:
            result = result * base % mod
        base = base * base % mod
        exp >>= 1
    return result

# nCr mod prime (Fermat's little theorem: inv = pow(x, p-2, p))
def precompute_factorials(n, mod):
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % mod
    inv_fact[n] = pow(fact[n], mod - 2, mod)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) % mod
    return fact, inv_fact

def nCr(n, r, fact, inv_fact, mod):
    if r < 0 or r > n: return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % mod * inv_fact[n-r] % mod

# Chinese Remainder Theorem (for coprime moduli)
def crt(remainders, moduli):
    M = 1
    for m in moduli: M *= m
    x = 0
    for r, m in zip(remainders, moduli):
        Mi = M // m
        x += r * Mi * pow(Mi, -1, m)   # Python 3.8+ pow with -1 for modular inverse
    return x % M
whenToUse: Large powers mod prime, combinations mod p (nCr), Fermat's little theorem, modular inverse.

name: KMP, String Matching
description: Knuth-Morris-Pratt finds all occurrences of a pattern in a text in O(n+m) by precomputing a failure function that avoids redundant comparisons.
whenToUse: String search in O(n+m), find pattern in text, check if s2 is rotation of s1 (search in s1+s1), strStr().

name: Rabin-Karp Rolling Hash
description: Hash the pattern and slide a window over the text, recomputing the hash in O(1) per step via a rolling formula. Average O(n+m).
template:
def rabin_karp(text, pattern):
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    BASE, MOD = 31, 10**9 + 7

    def poly_hash(s, length):
        h = 0
        for i in range(length):
            h = (h * BASE + ord(s[i]) - ord('a') + 1) % MOD
        return h

    ph = poly_hash(pattern, m)
    th = poly_hash(text, m)
    power = pow(BASE, m - 1, MOD)   # BASE^(m-1) for removal
    matches = []
    if th == ph and text[:m] == pattern: matches.append(0)

    for i in range(1, n - m + 1):
        # Roll: remove leftmost char, add new rightmost char
        th = (th - (ord(text[i-1]) - ord('a') + 1) * power) % MOD
        th = (th * BASE + ord(text[i+m-1]) - ord('a') + 1) % MOD
        th %= MOD
        if th == ph and text[i:i+m] == pattern:
            matches.append(i)
    return matches

# Longest Duplicate Substring (binary search + rolling hash)
def longest_dup_sub(s):
    def has_dup(length):
        BASE, MOD = 31, 2**61 - 1
        power = pow(BASE, length, MOD)
        h = 0
        for ch in s[:length]: h = (h * BASE + ord(ch)) % MOD
        seen = {h}
        for i in range(length, len(s)):
            h = (h * BASE + ord(s[i]) - (ord(s[i-length]) * power)) % MOD
            if h in seen: return True
            seen.add(h)
        return False
    lo, hi, ans = 0, len(s), ""
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if has_dup(mid): lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return ans
whenToUse: Find pattern in text, find duplicate substrings, longest duplicate substring (binary search + rolling hash), 2D pattern matching.

name: Manacher's Algorithm
description: Finds the longest palindromic substring in O(n) by exploiting mirror symmetry of palindromes already found.
template:
def manacher(s):
    # Transform s to handle even-length palindromes
    # "abc" → "#a#b#c#"
    t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
    n = len(t)
    p = [0] * n    # p[i] = radius of palindrome centered at i
    center = right = 0

    for i in range(n):
        if i < right:
            mirror = 2 * center - i
            p[i] = min(right - i, p[mirror])
        # Try to expand
        while (i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + p[i] + 1 < n
               and t[i - p[i] - 1] == t[i + p[i] + 1]):
            p[i] += 1
        # Update center and right boundary
        if i + p[i] > right:
            center, right = i, i + p[i]

    # Longest palindrome
    max_len, center_idx = max((v, i) for i, v in enumerate(p))
    start = (center_idx - max_len) // 2
    return s[start: start + max_len]

def count_palindromes(s):
    t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
    n, p = len(t), [0] * len(t)
    center = right = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if i < right: p[i] = min(right-i, p[2*center-i])
        while i-p[i]-1>=0 and i+p[i]+1<n and t[i-p[i]-1]==t[i+p[i]+1]: p[i]+=1
        if i+p[i]>right: center, right = i, i+p[i]
    return sum(v // 2 + 1 for v in p)
whenToUse: Longest palindromic substring, count palindromic substrings in O(n), palindrome partitioning.

name: Z-Algorithm
description: Computes Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s. Equivalent power to KMP.
whenToUse: Pattern matching (concatenate pattern + # + text, look for Z[i] = len(pattern)), string period detection.

name: Bellman-Ford
description: Shortest path for graphs with negative edges. Relax all edges V-1 times. Can detect negative cycles.
whenToUse: Negative edge weights, detect negative cycles, currency arbitrage, cheapest flights with K stops.

name: Floyd-Warshall
description: All-pairs shortest path via DP. dist[i][j] updated by routing through intermediate node k.
whenToUse: All-pairs shortest path, detect negative cycles, transitive closure, find the diameter of a graph.

name: Tarjan's, Bridges & SCCs
description: Tarjan's algorithm finds bridges, articulation points, and strongly connected components (SCCs) in one DFS pass using discovery times and low-link values.
whenToUse: Find bridges (critical connections), articulation points, SCCs in directed graph, 2-SAT.

name: Kruskal's MST
description: Minimum Spanning Tree: sort edges by weight, greedily add edges that don't form a cycle (checked via Union-Find).
template:
def kruskal(n, edges):
    """edges: [(weight, u, v)]  Returns (total_weight, mst_edges)"""
    edges.sort()
    parent = list(range(n))
    rank   = [0] * n

    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path halving
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    def union(x, y):
        px, py = find(x), find(y)
        if px == py: return False
        if rank[px] < rank[py]: px, py = py, px
        parent[py] = px
        if rank[px] == rank[py]: rank[px] += 1
        return True

    total, mst = 0, []
    for w, u, v in edges:
        if union(u, v):
            total += w
            mst.append((u, v, w))
            if len(mst) == n - 1:
                break          # MST complete
    return total, mst
whenToUse: Minimum cost to connect all nodes, network design, clustering, Borůvka.

name: Segment Tree
description: Binary tree where each node stores aggregate of a range. Supports O(log n) point updates and range queries (sum, min, max).
whenToUse: Range sum/min/max queries with updates, count inversions, falling squares, rectangle area.

name: Fenwick Tree (BIT)
description: Binary Indexed Tree supports O(log n) prefix sum queries and point updates with less code than a Segment Tree.
timeComplexity: O(log n) per update/query, O(n log n) build
whenToUse: Prefix sum with updates, count of smaller numbers after self, 2D BIT for 2D range sums, inversions.

name: Kadane's Algorithm
description: Maximum subarray sum in O(n). Extend current subarray or start fresh when running sum goes negative.
whenToUse: Maximum subarray (Leetcode 53), maximum circular subarray, maximum product subarray (modified).
intuition: Walk the array tracking the best subarray ending right here. At each element you either extend the previous best or start fresh: best = max(x, best + x), and you keep the global max. It's dynamic programming compressed into one variable, O(n) time and O(1) space.

name: Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm
description: Find the majority element (appears > n/2 times) in O(n) time and O(1) space. Maintain a candidate and cancel it with different elements.
template:
# Majority element (> n/2)
def majority_element(nums):
    candidate, count = None, 0
    for num in nums:
        if count == 0:
            candidate = num
        count += 1 if num == candidate else -1
    # Optional: verify candidate actually has majority
    return candidate

# Elements appearing > n/3 times (at most 2 candidates)
def majority_element_n3(nums):
    c1, c2, cnt1, cnt2 = None, None, 0, 0
    for num in nums:
        if num == c1:   cnt1 += 1
        elif num == c2: cnt2 += 1
        elif cnt1 == 0: c1, cnt1 = num, 1
        elif cnt2 == 0: c2, cnt2 = num, 1
        else:           cnt1 -= 1; cnt2 -= 1
    n = len(nums)
    return [c for c in (c1, c2) if nums.count(c) > n // 3]
whenToUse: Majority element, find element appearing > n/3 times (two candidates variant).

name: Dutch National Flag / 3-Way Partition
description: Dijkstra's 3-way partition: sort an array with 3 distinct values (0/1/2) in-place in one pass using three pointers: low, mid, high.
whenToUse: Sort colors (Leetcode 75), 3-way quicksort pivot partition, partition array by multiple conditions.

name: QuickSelect
description: Find the k-th smallest element in average O(n) using the partition step from QuickSort.
template:
import random

def quick_select(nums, k):
    """Returns the k-th smallest element (0-indexed k)."""
    def partition(lo, hi):
        pivot_idx = random.randint(lo, hi)
        nums[pivot_idx], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[pivot_idx]
        pivot = nums[hi]
        i = lo
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if nums[j] <= pivot:
                nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
                i += 1
        nums[i], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[i]
        return i

    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        p = partition(lo, hi)
        if p == k:   return nums[p]
        elif p < k:  lo = p + 1
        else:        hi = p - 1
    return nums[lo]

# K-th largest = (n-k)-th smallest
def kth_largest(nums, k):
    return quick_select(nums, len(nums) - k)
timeComplexity: O(n) average, O(n²) worst (use random pivot)
whenToUse: K-th largest/smallest element, median of unsorted array.

name: Sweep Line
description: Process events sorted by position (left to right). Track active intervals/points using a sorted structure or heap.
template:
# Maximum overlap at any point (e.g. meeting rooms)
def max_overlap(intervals):
    events = []
    for start, end in intervals:
        events.append((start, 1))    # +1 at start
        events.append((end,  -1))   # -1 at end
    events.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))  # tie-break: end before start
    active = max_active = 0
    for _, delta in events:
        active += delta
        max_active = max(max_active, active)
    return max_active

# Skyline problem
import heapq
def get_skyline(buildings):
    events = []
    for l, r, h in buildings:
        events.append((l, -h, r))   # entering (negative height for max-heap trick)
        events.append((r,  0, 0))   # leaving
    events.sort()
    result = []
    heap = [(0, float('inf'))]      # (neg_height, right_boundary)
    for x, neg_h, r in events:
        if neg_h != 0:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (neg_h, r))
        while heap[0][1] <= x:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        max_h = -heap[0][0]
        if not result or result[-1][1] != max_h:
            result.append([x, max_h])
    return result
whenToUse: Area of rectangles, rectangle overlap, skyline problem, maximum CPU load, minimum platforms.

name: Binary Search Tree (BST)
description: A binary tree holding the invariant: every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger. That ordering gives O(height) search, insert, and delete.
intuition: It's binary search turned into a tree: at each node go left if your target is smaller, right if larger, halving what's left each step. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) visits the values in sorted order, that's the trick behind 'kth smallest' and 'validate BST'. Balanced it's O(log n); but inserting already-sorted data makes it degenerate into a linked list at O(n), which is exactly why real systems use self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) or B-trees.
whenToUse: Ordered data needing fast insert/delete/lookup; kth-smallest, range queries, or iterating a tree in sorted order.
template:
def search_bst(root, target):
    node = root
    while node:
        if target == node.val: return node
        node = node.left if target < node.val else node.right
    return None

def inorder(root, out):        # yields values in sorted order
    if not root: return
    inorder(root.left, out)
    out.append(root.val)
    inorder(root.right, out)
timeComplexity: O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst

name: B-Tree / B+Tree
description: A balanced search tree where each node holds many keys and has many children (high fan-out), kept deliberately shallow. It's the structure behind almost every database and filesystem index.
intuition: Take a BST and let each node hold hundreds of keys instead of one, so the tree is very wide and only 3 to 4 levels deep even for billions of rows. Why hundreds? Each node is sized to one disk page/block, so a single disk read pulls in a whole node full of keys, minimizing the expensive part (disk seeks). You binary-search within a node, then descend to the right child. A B+Tree keeps all actual values in the leaves and links the leaves in a chain, so range scans (WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30) become a fast sequential walk. That fan-out-for-fewer-disk-reads is why databases index with B-trees rather than plain BSTs.
whenToUse: Understanding database and filesystem indexes; why disk-based structures maximize fan-out; when queries do range scans. (Pairs with the System Design concept 'Storage Engines: B-Tree vs LSM-Tree'.)
template:
# Conceptual, not interview code:
#  - node holds up to M keys and M+1 child pointers (M ~ hundreds, = 1 disk page)
#  - keys within a node are sorted; children partition the key ranges between them
#  - all leaves at the same depth  -> the tree stays balanced
#  - B+Tree: values live only in leaves, leaves linked  -> O(log n) point + fast range scans
#  - height ~ log_M(n), so even billions of rows are ~3-4 disk reads deep
